results.title: 2025 Tariffs on Electronics from China: Design and Source Smarter
results.content:
NOTE: This article was updated on July 3, 2025 to reflect recent information regarding tariffs.

The tariff tables have turned — again. If your designs depend on Chinese components, your cost projections may already be out of date.

Tariffs on electronics from China are once again reshaping the landscape for U.S. manufacturers. In 2025, the Trump administration revived aggressive trade tactics — including steep import duties aimed at reducing reliance on Chinese supply chains. [...] Tariffs are just one part of the risk landscape. To fully protect your supply chain:

 Invest in demand forecasting to avoid overstocking tariffed components
 Gather and verify Certificates of Origin for all suppliers
 Shorten logistics chains where possible to avoid transit disruptions
 Embed life cycle planning into design to prevent unexpected part shortages

These practices help build long-term stability, even as policy changes continue unfolding. [...] In 2025, tariffs are proving to be a profound destabilizing force, deeply affecting engineering, procurement, and production operations.

Key impacts include:

 Unit cost increases of 15% or more on affected items
 Surprise customs fees that appear after delivery due to retroactive audits or classification shifts
 Longer lead times from enhanced inspection protocols and customs delays
 Supply chain disruptions if a vendor can’t pivot to alternative, tariff-compliant sourcing in time

results.title: Chain Reaction: US Tariffs and Global Supply Chains
results.content: Tariff uncertainty: Manufacturing firms today face mixed messages on US trade goals and high uncertainty about long-term tariff levels. Maximizing tariff revenues requires the US to have low enough tariffs to preserve import volumes, but incentivizing onshoring to the US requires very high tariffs in strategic sectors. Inflation management and China de-risking are additional considerations. In short, until US goals are clarified, firms will find it hard to plan around future tariff levels. [...] However, if the US phases in tariffs on Chinese content or otherwise provides exemptions for companies diversifying, it will create a significant incentive for companies to build up ex-China production of intermediate inputs and components. [...] Supply chains tend to move when goods can be manufactured in countries with lower “landed costs”—the cost of production plus shipping, customs duties, and insurance. Tariffs directly impact these calculations, which helps explain why US imports from China declined after the US imposed Section 301 tariffs on $550 billion of imports from China in 2017 (Figure 1).  Supply chain assessment: We evaluate your supply chain — from raw material to finished product — to identify risks and opportunities.
 Supplier scouting: We search for and connect you with qualified domestic suppliers.

 Process improvement: We apply lean practices to improve production and reduce costs.
 Technology automation: We analyze and help implement appropriate technologies. [...] As global trade evolves, manufacturers — either directly or indirectly — may face new challenges, such as adjusting pricing strategies, disrupting supply chains, and rising production expenses.

However, you can manage your risk and reduce your tariff burden through expert guidance and strategic solutions:

## Alternative Tariff Strategies [...] Foreign trade zones: Manufacture domestically while deferring or reducing duties based on the final product classification.
 First sale rule: Pay duties based on the manufacturer or middleman price (rather than the importer price).
